records.content: Mock Drafts Positional Rankings NFL News Odds Betting Newsletter STATE Florida dengue cases surge to 485 in largest outbreak in US in decades Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 30, 2026, 10:18 a.m. ET Here are symptoms of dengue fever you should watch for. How can you reduce the chances of getting mosquito-transmitted diseases in Florida? Florida reported 60 more locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 485 for the year as of Oct. 24, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which has 385 confirmed cases. Locally acquired cases have now been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to extend a state of local emergency to Nov. 5 in the county as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has popped up this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Another case of West Nile Virus was reported in Sarasota County, bringing the 2026 total to seven cases, although two were asymptomatic. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 18 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases increasing in Florida, with more counties reporting mosquito-transmitted disease According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 24, there have been 485 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in 12 counties, up from 425 cases reported Oct. 17. There have also been six positive samples of locally acquired of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 485 cases 385 in Hillsborough County 67 in Pinellas County 9 in Miami-Dade County 9 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: seven cases 2 in Alachua County 1 in Duval County (asymptomatic blood donors) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? A local state of emergency has been extended in Hillsborough County until Nov. 5. A state of local emergency can be in effect for only seven days, unless rescinded or extended, according to the Hillsborough County Department of Health. "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Trump wants mosquitoes, ticks eliminated in Washington, D.C. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order to eliminate ticks and mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. The order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Administrator of General Services, along with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, to "develop and implement a campaign across Washington, D.C., to reduce invasive mosquito populations by 90 percent and the tick population by 50 percent by 2028 using safe and effective, non-chemical, and innovative technology-enabled methods. "This new model, localized to Washington, D.C., can later be applied nationwide as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. records.content: News Health Four dengue cases detected in Rawalpindi in two days — Dawn UA.NEWS 01 November 2026 06:57 In Rawalpindi, Pakistan, four new dengue cases have been confirmed over the past two days. Since the start of the current season, the number of registered patients has reached 83, Dawn reports . According to district disease prevention officer Dr Jawad, three positive serological test results for the dengue virus were received on Friday and one more on Saturday. 29 wards at very high risk as dengue could turn severe in Dhaka South Staff Correspondent Published: 04 November 2026, 19:08 শেয়ার করুন: Graphics: Agamir Somoy Authorities have expressed concern that the spread of dengue and chikungunya could take a severe turn in areas under the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC). A joint survey by DSCC and the Communicable Disease Control (CDC) unit found on Wednesday that mosquito density in all 75 wards of DSCC exceeds the normal index. Of these, 29 wards have been classified as being at very high risk. Aedes mosquitoes were found to breed most frequently in regular residential houses and high-rise buildings rather than under construction or semi pucca buildings. The 12-day survey was conducted from September 27 to October 8 by 36 field workers from DSCC and the Communicable Disease Control (CDC) unit of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). The Kobo Toolbox technology was used to ensure accurate data collection. Using scientific and random sampling methods, the survey teams visited 2,250 houses, selecting 30 houses from each of DSCC’s 75 wards. After completing the survey, the collected data were analyzed to identify potential dengue hotspots. The survey found Aedes mosquito larvae and pupae in 803 of the 2,250 houses inspected. Individual houses accounted for the largest share of breeding sources, with larvae found in 31.37 percent of them. Larvae were also found in 31.06 percent of high-rise buildings, 17.39 percent of semi pucca houses, 14.11 percent of vacant plots and 13.04 percent of buildings under construction. Among the containers and locations where larvae were found, stagnant water on floors accounted for the highest share at 12.26 percent. Buckets accounted for 10.34 percent and plastic drums for 8.89 percent. Based on larval density, DSCC classified 29 wards as very high risk, 28 as moderate risk and 18 as general risk areas. Following the survey findings, the city corporation has already launched special mosquito control drives in high-risk areas. DSCC authorities said dengue cannot be completely eliminated through government or city corporation initiatives alone. Residents must keep their homes and workplaces clean and develop the habit of removing stagnant clean water at least once a week. The corporation also expects strong public cooperation and an active role from the media in building a dengue free and livable city. Meanwhile, DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam said mosquito control activities were being intensified by identifying high risk areas. “According to the survey findings, mosquito control activities are being intensified. However, dengue cannot be controlled by spraying insecticides alone. Public awareness is essential,” he said. PHOTO BY NICOLE DROEGER Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that’s raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile, Zika and dengue fever. Florida’s struggles with dengue fever in 2026 should be a warning. Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, had seen more than 350 dengue cases, at least one of them fatal, by late October. Miami-Dade County had reported more than 200 cases, and the statewide number was still rising in what has been described as the largest dengue outbreak in modern Florida history. There has also been a case in Sarasota County with a woman who was hospitalized, during which time she was extremely sick and lost 17 pounds. More than 400 of the over 700 Florida cases, including many of those in Hillsborough County and at least seven in the Orlando area, were listed as locally acquired from mosquitoes in the area. Climate change is part of the reason people in many parts of the country are seeing more mosquitoes. Rising global temperatures and shorter winters expand the area suitable for mosquitoes to live in and transmit viruses that cause diseases. Climate change also brings increasingly erratic storm systems, heat and rainfall patterns that leave standing water, creating conditions ideal for mosquitoes to breed. The other major factor shaping where mosquitoes live, often overlooked, is humans themselves. We study entomology and medical geography, including the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. To understand why you may be seeing more mosquitoes, and why communities like Hillsborough County are spending millions of dollars on attempts to control them, start by looking close to home. MOSQUITOS FOLLOW HUMANS Mosquitoes such as Aedes aegypti — the primary transmitter of pathogens that cause dengue fever, yellow fever, Chikungunya and Zika in the Americas — likely arrived in the U.S. with the slave trade. Both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, a transmitter of many of the same diseases but a more recent arrival in the U.S., are moved by the global shipping network, which can take them to new locations and reintroduce them in parts of their ranges where they may have been controlled in the past. Aedes aegypti’s habits, including its ability to use household environments for living and breeding, have made it a very successful and established invader where climate conditions permit. A flowerpot saucer, clogged gutter, discarded tire, birdbath or even a bottle cap can collect enough water for mosquito larvae to develop. A single Aedes aegypti mosquito can lay more than 100 eggs at a time up to five times during its lifespan, which is only about a month. As suburban neighborhoods expand, so do opportunities for mosquitoes to breed and find humans for their meals. Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people. This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development. Aedes albopictus, originally native to Southeast Asia and now found in all habitable continents, provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes arrived in the U.S. mostly because of human actions. They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo. Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the interstate highway system. By 2017, Aedes albopictus was documented in 1,368 counties across 40 states, and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S. One of Iowa’s first established Aedes albopictus populations, for example, appeared in the Des Moines metropolitan area, where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities. Its spread from Southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes. MOST COMMON THREAT: WEST NILE West Nile virus remains the most widespread mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States. It is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country. Culex mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states. Because Culex mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease. Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus lengthened by an average of 20 days between 1999 and 2024. A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. Just recently, Sarasota County confirmed had a recent case of West Nile. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year. In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that Aedes mosquitoes could remain active late into the year. Florida saw a rise in dengue cases. Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial. records.content: Another health outbreak is on the loose. This time, Florida is the state most heavily impacted. Videos by Wide Open Country According to a Monday (November 2) report from Fox News Digital, Florida Health Officials have confirmed 485 "locally acquired" cases of Dengue Fever in the Sunshine State. They have defined the outbreak as the largest in years (via The New York Post). Several Cases of Dengue Fever Reported in Florida Per the report, Florida health officials logged 60 new cases of the virus between October 18 and October 24. The largest number of new cases came from Tampa Bay. The city accounted for more than 90% of the new cases. Additionally, more than 300 "travel-associated" cases of Dengue Fever were reported in the state earlier in 2026. Following the release of the report, there was a bevy of reactions on social media. "And just like that, they have their excuse lined up for more genetically engineered mosquitoes to be dropped in Florida," one user wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter. "Funny how [Dengue] spread exactly where they released the genetically modified mosquitoes to stop dengue, but it's just a conspiracy theory, not a coincidence," a second user chimed in. "I don't trust anything dealing with this government," a third user remarked. New Virus Derives From Mosquitoes Dengue fever is an illness from mosquito bites that happens in tropical and subtropical areas of the world (via Mayo Clinic). The Aedes mosquito is the most recognizable carrier of the virus. It can cause a high fever and flu-like symptoms. "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health told Fox News Digital. The spokesperson also added: "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk." Other symptoms can include - Headache. - Muscle, bone, or joint pain. - Upset stomach. - Vomiting. - Pain behind the eyes. - Swollen glands. - Rash. A more serious form of dengue fever, called dengue hemorrhagic fever, can cause bleeding, a sudden drop in blood pressure, and death. Symptoms of the more serious form of dengue fever include: - Bad stomach pain. - Repeated vomiting. - Bleeding from the gums or nose. - Blood in the urine, stools, or vomit. - Bleeding under the skin, which might look like bruising. - Hard or fast breathing. - Tiredness. - Being cranky or restless. Those experiencing those symptoms should immediately seek medical attention
